title: I’m a Game Graphic Artist, and I used AI to help me build a custom isometric map tool in Unity.
author: Fun-Medium4482
selftext:
It started because I needed a map editor for some isometric pixel art I was making. I just wanted a tool that is comfortable for an artist to use, so I focused heavily on emphasizing visual elements in the UI.

My goal wasn't just to make a quick demo, but to build a fully functional tool that I could actually use for my own real development and art projects.

The biggest challenge was the technical implementation, since I didn't write the code myself. I built the entire system—over 140k lines of C# **(mostly UI and tool-related code)**—using code generated by Claude. I acted purely as the director and QA, testing the technical output and giving constant feedback to get the right code that matched my design intentions.

To showcase the tool, I also wanted to test out Remotion (a framework for making videos programmatically). I asked AI to write the video copy for me, and used Remotion to put the presentation together.

Please understand that since I am not a developer, I won't be able to explain the specific code or underlying system logic in detail. Also, I am not very fluent in English, so I am using a translator to write this post.

Thanks for reading!

comments.author: NirinA-xyz
comments.body: Impressive! Will you release your tool for others in the future? Or is it just for yourself?

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body: Thank you! I'm still constantly improving it, but since I'm not actually a developer, I'm still just studying and learning as I go. Because of that, I don't have any plans to release it right now. Honestly, building this has just made me realize how truly amazing real developers are!

replies.author: yecats131
replies.body:
You should consider putting this on GitHub. Just make a note in the README that it's 100% vibe coded and may or may not be updated. If you set the license to something like MIT or CC0 then people can make copies of it and iterate on their own. 


(This assumes you don't intend to sell it, based on your comments.)



Since you aren't a dev: GitHub is a place people put the source code for projects. You can make an account then just tell AI to do it all for you.

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482

comments.author: Kiryoko
comments.body:
Awesome job!

Out of curiosity, did you have any software development/programming experience before building this using Claude?

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body:
Thank you! I actually have no software development or programming experience. However, I do have a lot of experience learning and using various tools.

I've also been using Claude since the paid subscription came out, so this kind of workflow wasn't too unfamiliar to me. Plus, my past experience communicating with different departments in real-world projects really helped me figure out how to effectively 'communicate' with Claude to get the results I wanted

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body: Thank you, that means a lot!

comments.author: DatabaseConstant7870
comments.body: Does this work for 3D games? I’m trying to figure out a pipeline for rooms in houses to be generated already laid out and not just furniture clustered in the center of each room

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body: Thanks for the interest! Actually, this tool is specifically designed for 2D isometric pixel art, so it doesn't support 3D environments or 3D pipelines at the moment. Since I'm focusing on an artist-friendly workflow for 2D projects, the logic is tied to that specific perspective. However, I am planning to dive into 3D for my next project. I’m still figuring out if it will be a tool or something else.

comments.author: mr_dudo
comments.body: hey bro, im not familiar with unity but i do want to start using ai to create a game, this is a tool that is used inside of uinity or did the ai made the entire thing im seeing? like the algorith for the people to walk, etc

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body: Unity provides the foundation, and I used AI to script the behaviors like how people walk

comments.author: Recent_Stop17
comments.body: Are characters, animations, and backgrounds also created using AI? If so, using a map editor would drastically shorten the graphics work.

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body: The characters, animations, and backgrounds were actually hand-drawn. The primary purpose of the map tool is for ease of placement, pathfinding, and data management. I haven't personally experienced a tool that can fully implement everything you mentioned just yet. (I have used AI to generate references for the final output, but even then, I always had to do manual retouching before using them. I feel that pixel art is particularly difficult in this regard.)

comments.author: Awkward_Champion6957
comments.body: Human and machine working together. Now that's what I like to see with AI. Also a product made that you can see a use for not just bad art or okay apps that already exist. Well done!

replies.author: Fun-Medium4482
replies.body:
Thank you! I actively used AI to achieve the exact visuals I wanted, and I am absolutely thrilled with the results. Rather than feeling like 'AI is doing everything for me,' it felt more like a collaborative partner that helped me visually express and communicate my ideas.

The best part was that AI allowed me to step beyond just the artwork and dip my toes into the technical side, which really broadened my perspective on the project as a whole. For instance, I implemented pathfinding logic with AI's help, and it was my very first time learning how it actually works under the hood.

Understanding the technical mechanisms behind the scenes made it so much easier to pinpoint exactly what needed to be modified in the art and how to strike the right balance with the details.
